Abstract
Multi-area economic dispatch (MAED) provides an indispensable component for the secu­
rity and economic operation of contemporary power systems. Over recent years, numerous 
metaheuristic optimization algorithms (MOAs) have surfaced for addressing the MAED 
problem. However, none of the literature to date conducted a comprehensive statistical 
research work on the MAED problem. In part I of this series, we present a comprehen­
sive survey on this problem. (1) We collect all eleven reported MAED cases studied over 
the years. These cases have different structures, scales, and constraints. We illustrate the 
structures of all cases and provide their corresponding system parameters. (2) We collect 
all the MOA solution algorithms. These algorithms are inspired by different ways, and we 
categorize them in detail and review them comprehensively. (3) We list the detailed ap­
plications of MOAs on different cases and count the percentage of studies on each case. 
(4) Finally, we summarize the current research progress and point out the future research 
directions in terms of MAED models and solution methods, respectively. This survey pro­
vides an extensive overview of the MAED cases and its solution methods. It can provide 
applicable and reference suggestions for future research on the MAED problem.

1  Introduction
Electricity, a highly versatile and easily transmitted form of energy, profoundly impacts var­
ious aspects of human activity. Recent years have seen a dramatic rise in electricity demand, 
driven by the rapid expansion of global industry. This escalating thirst for electrical power 
has precipitated apprehensions on excessive energy consumption, soaring production costs, 
and pressing issue of climate change. Consequently, there is a pressing need for economic 
evaluation of fossil fuel utilization, availability, and security. Within this framework, the 
economic dispatch (ED) of power systems, characterized by its multi-constraint optimiza­
tion nature, emerges as a critical area of research (Spangler and Shoults 2014).
ED describes the optimal dispatching of grid-connected generation units without vio­
lating various system constraints to address load demand and minimize fuel costs. (Yang 
et al. 1996). Typically, ED is characterized by its complex optimization nature, marked 
by non-convex and non-linear properties and substantial dimensionality. This complexity 
is primarily attributed to operational constraints of generating units, including multi-fuel 
options (MFO), prohibited operation zones (POZ), valve point effects (VPE), ramp rate 
limits (RRL) and transmission loss (TL) (Cai et al. 2012).
As electricity demand continues to rise, the interconnection of previously independent 
small-scale power systems has become increasingly common, enhancing electricity uti­
lization and system resilience. Consequently, the traditional single-area ED methods are 
insufficient for addressing the needs of multi-area economic dispatch (MAED). The MAED 
framework, which incorporates power exchanges between interconnected areas, holds sub­
stantial practical significance. This extended form of ED is inherently more complex, as 
it must simultaneously satisfy power transmission constraints across tie lines and manage 
system constraints within each area (Basu 2014; Mokarram et al. 2018). The complexity 
escalates further when factoring in MFO and VPE in extensive power systems.
The complexity of solving the ED problem is significantly exacerbated by the presence 
of MFO and VPE, making it an extremely challenging task. Consequently, researchers have 
continuously explored and proposed various methods to address this problem. Historically, 
traditional mathematical approaches, including numerical method (Lin and Viviani 1984), 
linear programming (Wu et al. 2016; Pan et al. 2020), nonlinear programming (Zhu 2003), 
Lagrangian relaxation (Hemamalini and Simon 2009; Li et al. 2013), quadratic program­
ming (Reid and Hasdorff 1973; Mclarty et al. 2019), dynamic programming (Liang and 
Glover 1992), etc., were utilized as a solution to the ED problem. Those mathematical meth­
ods offer the advantages of rigorous mathematical derivation and high computational effi­
ciency. However, each method comes with specific limitations that affect its effectiveness. 
For instance, linear programming, which relies on linearizing the objective function, can 
introduce significant errors (Wu et al. 2016). Nonlinear programming requires differentiable 
objective functions, which limits its applicability in more complex scenarios (Coelho and 
Mariani 2006; Goncalves et al. 2019). Dynamic programming, despite its computational

Unlike traditional mathematical methods, modern metaheuristic optimization algorithms 
(MOAs) do not impose strict requirements on the mathematical modeling of optimization 
problems, nor do they necessitate the objective function to be continuous or differentia­
ble. Additionally, MOAs exhibit strong global convergence capabilities, which make them 
well-suited for providing optimal or near-optimal solutions to the ED problem (Coelho and 
Mariani 2006; Sayah and Hamouda 2013; Dai et al. 2022; Liu et al. 2022a). Compared 
with traditional mathematical optimization algorithms, MOAs present several advantages: 
(i) they do not rely on gradient computation; (ii) they are not constrained by numerous 
mathematical limitations; (iii) they offer a broader range of applicability; and (iv) they pos­
sess robust global search capabilities. However, it is essential to acknowledge the inherent 
limitations of MOAs. A significant drawback is the absence of a strong theoretical guarantee 
for reaching the global optimum consistently. For a MOA, different runs of a same problem 
may yield varying local minima especially for non-convex problems, which diminishes the 
reliability and practicality of MOAs in certain applications. Nevertheless, ongoing research 
has introduced various techniques to mitigate these issues, resulting in the growing accep­
tance of MOAs in power system optimization. Consequently, researchers have increasingly 
turned to MOAs for solving the ED problem, utilizing algorithms such as particle swarm 
optimization (PSO) (Jeyakumar et al. 2006; Neyestani et al. 2010; Chen et al. 2018, 2020), 
differential evolution (DE) (Liu et al. 2022b, 2021; Li et al. 2019; Hamdi et al. 2019), 
teaching–learning based optimization (TLBO) (Prakash et al. 2018; Banerjee et al. 2015), 
marine predators algorithm (MPA) (Shaheen et al. 2022; Pan et al. 2022), crisscross search 
optimization (CSO) (Tang et al. 2022; Meng et al. 2015), and cuckoo search (CS) (Luo and 
Yu 2022; Huang et al. 2020; Nguyen et al. 2018; Basu and Chowdhury 2013).
The initial application of MOAs to the MAED problem dates back to as early as 2000 
(Jayabarathi and Ramachandran 2000). However, the early years saw limited application 
due to insufficient focus on MAED and the nascent state of the technology. It was not 
until around 2010, and particularly after 2015, that MOAs received substantial attention 
and experienced rapid advancement. Concurrently, the models for MAED began to evolve, 
becoming increasingly sophisticated and varied during this period.
Recently, several literatures have made related reviews on the MAED problem. For 
instance, Pattanaik et al. (2017) summarized DE, evolutionary programming (EP), genetic 
algorithm (GA), and simulated annealing (SA) for solving this problem. Kunya et al. (2023) 
conducted a simple review of recent advances in ED and MAED problems. Girishkumar 
et al. (2021) reviewed the application of GA to the problem. Sharifian et al. ( 2024) pro­
vided a review of solution methods for the MAED problem, addressed key research, and 
explored the associated challenges. Although these reviews offer valuable insights into the 
MAED problem and its solutions, several areas require further elaboration and refinement.

(1)	 A comprehensive and clear framework of MAED research is presented. This includes a 
detailed account of research developments over time from both a solutions and models 
perspective, along with a well-defined historical trajectory of MAED research.
(2)	 Solution methods are extensively reviewed. This survey offers a thorough examination

and systematically classifies these methods based on established criteria.
(3)	 MAED cases are meticulously summarized. The review compiles a complete statistical

and a detailed description of their system structures, providing a valuable reference for

2  Formulation of MAED problem
The primary goal of MAED is to achieve the minimization of the aggregate fuel costs across 
the entire power system. This is accomplished by optimizing the generation allocation 
within each distinct area and managing the inter-area power exchanges, all while adhering 
to a series of critical operational constraints (Ghasemi et al. 2016). Figure 1 illustrates a 
representative configuration of a four-area MAED system.

3.3  Case III: 2-areas with 40-units
This case introduces additional complexities, such as VPE, POZ, and RRL, making it sig­
nificantly more challenging for solvers. Both areas consist of 20 generating units each, with 
load demands of 7500 MW and 3000 MW. The tie line’s upper limit is 1500 MW, as illus­

3.4  Case IV: 2-areas with 120-units
A larger system is represented in this case, featuring two areas with 70 and 50 generators, 
and load demands of 18,200 MW and 9,800 MW, respectively. The tie line’s capacity is 
limited to 2,000 MW. Detailed system characteristic parameters are provided in Fig. 8 and 
Table 9.
3.5  Case V: 2-areas with 140-units
Derived from a South Korean power system, this case involves 140 generating units evenly 
distributed between two areas. While all units consider the RRL, only 12 units account 
for the VPE, and 4 units consider the POZ. The total system load is 49,342 MW, with 
34,539 MW and 14,803 MW allocated to the two areas. The tie line capacity limit is set at 
6000 MW, with system characteristics detailed in Fig. 9 and Tables 10, 11, 12.
3.6  Case VI:3-areas with 10-units
This case involves a three-area MAED system with VPE, MFO, and TL, making it a small 
yet complex problem due to the simultaneous inclusion of these constraints. The areas are 
equipped with 4, 3, and 3 generating units, with respective loads of 1,350 MW, 675 MW, 
and 675 MW. The interconnection is facilitated by three tie lines, each with a capacity limit 
of 100 MW, as depicted in Fig. 10. The system parameters and transmission loss coefficients 
are detailed in Tables 13, 14, 15.

4  Optimization techniques survey
Initially, Lin et al. (1991) began to involve research on the MAED problem in 1991. How­
ever, it was not until after 2015 that related research work proliferated. According to the 
inspiration principles-based classification criteria for MOAs in Mohamed et al. (2020), the 
application of various types of MOAs to the MAED problem is illustrated in Fig. 15.
4.1  Swarm intelligence techniques
Swarm Intelligence (SI) stands for a pivotal and formidable paradigm within the realm of 
computational intelligence. It derives inspiration in collective behavior observed in animals 
and social insects. In SI, each individual entity possesses its unique intelligence and behav­
ior. However, it is the synergy and integration of these individuals that endows SI with the 
formidable capability to address intricate and challenging problems (Mohamed et al. 2020). 
The fundamental characteristics of SI techniques can be succinctly summarized as follows: 
(i) Information is shared among multiple individuals; (ii) Self-organization and co-evolution 
capability of individuals; (iii) High efficiency of co-learning, and (iv) Easy parallelizability 
for solving practical and real-time problems (Hassanien and Emary 2018). For the MAED 
problem, the SI techniques were first applied in 2006. After 2015, its application had been 
rapidly developed (Jeyakumar et al. 2006; Sharma et al. 2010),59].
Wang et al. (2009) raised a modified multi-objective PSO based on local search to solve 
Case VII. Basu et al. (2013) used artificial bee colony (ABC) for solving Cases II, VI and 
VIII. Results comparing with DE, EP and GA showed that ABC yielded superior conver­
gence capability. Rani et al. (2014) investigated the effectiveness of PSO with exponentially 
varying inertia weight factor for solving Case VII. Basu (2014) introduced TLBO for solv­
ing Cases II, VI and VIII.
In (Jadoun et al. 2015a), an IPSO was proposed to solve Case VIII. IPSO enhances the 
cognitive aspect of particles’ velocity by leveraging prior experiences to uphold a harmoni­
ous equilibrium between social and cognitive behaviors. Subsequently, In (Jadoun et al. 
2015b), DCPSO incorporates the root mean square quantity of particles’ velocity in the 
control equation to improve the way the particles communicate, thus improving population 
diversity and preventing falling into local optimization. Simulation results on Case I and 
Case VIII indicated that DCPSO exhibits an enhanced capacity for addressing high-dimen­
sional MAED problems. Secui et al. (Secui 2015) suggested a chaotic global best artificial 
bee colony (CGABC) to Cases II, IV, VI, VII, and VIII.
Debua et al. (2016) applied backtracking search algorithm (BSA) to solve Cases III and V. 
BSA achieves the objective of finding the optimum through variation, crossover and selec­

VIII. Results demonstrated that FPA was outstanding concerning calculation efficiency, sta­
bility and solution quality. Basu (2016) suggested a quasi-oppositional group search opti­

4.2  Physics based techniques
Physics based technique is inspired by physical rules of the universe and the rules governing 
natural phenomenon (Biswas et al. 2013; Siddique and Adeli 2016). It was first applied to 
the MAED problem in 2009.
In (Jadoun et al. 2016), an improved fireworks algorithm (IFWA) was submitted for solv­
ing the MAED problem considering multiple fuels and other practical constraints. IFWA 
uses a limiting mapping operator and an adaptive dimension selection operator to enhance 
its effectiveness. The test results on Case VI showed that IFWA adapted well in solving this 
problem.
Yazdandoost et al. (2018) presented an electron search optimization algorithm (ESOA) 
inspired by electron movement mechanism for solving Case VIII. ESOA performed better 
over other algorithms with respect to accuracy and stability. In (Pattanaik et al. 2020), the 
simulated annealing showed its effectiveness on Case VIII. In (Li et al. 2017), the authors 
presented a modified chemical reaction optimization (PCRO) to solve Case VII. A novel 
coding mechanism is formulated to dynamically optimize its performance. Additionally, an 
adaptive neighborhood structure selection mechanism was integrated into PCRO to bolster 
search capabilities and preserve population diversity.
Sakthivel et al. (2020b) contributed a Coulomb’s and Franklin’s Laws Based Optimizer 
(CFLBO) for Cases II, VI and VII. CFLBO encompasses distinct stages, including attrac­
tion/repulsion, probabilistic ionization, and contact mechanisms. Comparative analysis 
against the exchange market optimization algorithm (EMA) indicated that CFLBO gets 
swifter convergence and superior fuel cost. In (Sakthivel and Sathya 2021c), a fuzzified 
CFLBO approach was further developed. It introduces a fuzzy decision strategy to search 
for the optimal combination of solutions in the Pareto optimal fronts set. Experiments were 
conducted on Case VI for two different scenarios. The results revealed that the fuzzified 
CFLBO provided a better compromise between optimal economic fuel cost and minimum 
emissions. Zare et al. (2021) presented a modified fireworks algorithm (IFW), which incor­
porates a cross-generation approach, along with a constraints-handling scheme to rectify 
potential solutions within the feasible search space. IFW was tested on three different sce­
narios of Cases VI and VIII, showing that IFW was capable of achieving better quality 
solutions.

(AIS) inspired by clonal selection for Cases II, VI and VIII. Basu (2014) applied TLBO to

Evolutionary techniques are primarily inspired by mimicking the evolutionary law of sur­

Jayabarathi et al. (2000) used EP to solve Case II and Case VII. Basu et al. (2005) pro­
posed a fast convergence EP (FCEP) for Cases II, VI and VIII. A comparative assessment 
with EP and improved fast EP (IFEP) indicated that the incorporation of Gaussian and Cau­
chy mutations can achieve better solutions.
Pandit et al. (2015) presented a fuzzy selection-based DE (DEFS) for the MAED prob­
lem considering reserve sharing. A fuzzy framework is adapted to mitigate the intricacies 
associated with multi-attribute decision-making in choosing succeeding population genera­
tion. DEFS was able to provide better solutions compared to PSO.
Li et al. (2018) proposed an efficient and powerful CSO combined with a Pareto multi-
objective processing strategy (MOCSO) for Case VIII. MOCSO applies two interacting 
algorithms based on horizontally and vertically crisscrossing to enhance global search 
and mitigate the risk of premature convergence. Simulation results showed that MOCSO 
obtained solutions superior to GBABC and NSGA-II.
Basu (2019a) suggested a nondominated genetic algorithm–II (NSGA-II) to the MAED 
problem, showing that it outperformed competitors. Besides, Basu (2019b) also suggested 
a chaotic FCEP (CFCEP) for solving Case VIII. With the tent chaotic sequence being used 
to adaptively adjust the scale factor, CFCEP gave significantly better results than FCEP.
In (Ikram et al. 2020), a polar bear optimization algorithm (PBOA) was applied for Case 
II. The primary benefit of the PBOA lies in its ability to maintain a balanced search agent 
size through the implementation of a dynamic control mechanism involving both agent 
elimination and growth.
Lin et al. (2023) proposed a data-driven agent-assisted approach named ELM-NSGA-II 
for solving Case VIII. It employs the support vector regression agent model in lieu of the 
conventional objective function and integrates knowledge distillation to reduce the time 
necessary for constructing the agent model.
Wang et al. (2024) introduced CLDE, an advanced variant of DE enhanced by a Com­
prehensive Learning Strategy (CLS), to solve six large-scale MAED problems. CLDE 
improves DE’s mutation and crossover strategies, along with a time-varying crossover rate 
strategy, which significantly balances both convergence speed and population diversity.

rithm (SLFA) and PSO, was submitted for solving Cases VI and VIII.
In (Mokarram et al. 2019a), JAYA-TLBO as a hybrid variant was put forward for Cases 
II, VI and VIII, showing that JAYA-TLBO improved the robustness and convergence speed 
for solving the MAED problem.
Elattar et al. (2020) submitted a hybrid algorithm of chaotic PSO and GA (HCPSOGA). 
HCPSOGA optimizes the parameters of CPSO by using GA. The effectiveness of HCP­
SOGA was tested on Cases VI and VIII. In (Chen and Imani 2020), the 140-units test system 
in Korea as Case X was extended and a hybrid ICA-PSO was introduced by using a PSO-
based search strategy to improve the position state of imperialist competitive algorithm 
(ICA). The hybrid PSO-ICA demonstrated exceptional performance in operation cost, fast 
convergence, and calculation efficiency for addressing large-scale MAED cases with non-
convex characteristics. Azizivahed et al. (2020b) submitted a hybrid algorithm (HGWO-
PSO) based on PSO and GWO. Comparison revealed that HGWO-PSO was able to improve 
approximately 3.1% and 3.3% in cost on Case VI and Case VIII, respectively.
Sharifian et al. (2023) proposed EMA-GOA by combining exchange market (GOA) and 
grasshopper optimization algorithm (EMA) for Cases II, III, and VI. EMA-GOA exhibited 
superior capabilities in reconciling exploration and exploitation through mitigating the issue 
of premature convergence in GOA.
Khalid et al. (2024) employed a hybrid optimization approach, combining the Crow 
Search Algorithm (CSA) and the JAYA Search Algorithm (JSA), referred to as CSA-JSA, 
to effectively solve Case VI.

4.6  Other techniques
In addition to the above MOAs, some non-MOAs also have a few applications to the MAED 
problem. For example, In (Streiffert 1995), an incremental network flow planning (INFP) 
method was introduced for Case VII. Yalcinoz et al. (1998) used a neural network (HNN) 
to solve Cases III and IV. Al-Sumait et al. (2008) used a pattern search (PS) that does not 
necessitate information concerning the gradient of the objective function for solving Case 
VII. REN et al. (2016) introduced centralized alternating direction methods (CSADM) for 
Cases III and VI, allowing the penalty parameters to be increased or decreased according to 
the information form each iteration. Results illustrated that CSADM significantly outper­
formed the conventional alternating direction method.
Qin et al. (2019) applied a newton-based distributed algorithm (NMDA) for Case VII. 
Mokarram et al. (2019b) proposed a straightforward parallel process approach called 
PMAED for Cases II and VIII. This approach decoupled regions by varying the amount of 
TCL for each tie line, and was verified in stability and convergence.
Yu et al. (2023) presented a Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL) architecture for 
Case VI in a fully offline optimization manner. The HRL architecture initiates the process 
by computing the scheduled area load in the upper layer with a Q-learning approach. Sub­
sequently, it derives a load-power table comprising optimal output power levels within indi­
vidual areas via a multi-stage decision algorithm in the lower layer. The application of the 
HRL architecture led to a reduction in fuel cost within the range of 0.01656% to 0.19173%.
5  Discussions
Part I of this series provides a detailed and comprehensive survey of the eleven studied cases 
of the MAED problem and the associated solving methods. By systematically reviewing the 
literature, we have summarized the relevant research and the application of various types 
of MOAs, as illustrated in Table 21 and Fig. 16 in chronological order. Additionally, the 
distribution of research focused on these cases is depicted in Fig. 17.
(1)	 Significant advancements in MAED research have been observed, particularly post-
2015. Before 2015, the application of MOAs to the MAED problem was limited due to 
the immaturity of the techniques and a general lack of attention. However, after 2015, 
the application of MOAs has rapidly developed and become widely adopted. Conse­
quently, MOAs have emerged as the predominant optimization technique for address­
ing the MAED problem.
(2)	 Swarm intelligence techniques have dominated MAED solutions, reflecting their 
adaptability and effectiveness. The application percentages of swarm intelligence tech­
niques, hybrid techniques, other techniques, evolutionary techniques, physics-based 
techniques, and human-related techniques in solving the MAED problem are 49.38%, 
14.81%, 12.35%, 11.11%, 8.64%, and 3.70%, respectively. This distribution highlights 
the extensive application of swarm intelligence techniques, particularly after 2015, 
whereas human-related techniques have seen the least use in addressing the MAED 
problem.

6  Conclusions and future works
Part I of this series presents a pioneering and systematic review of the MAED problem, 
encompassing a thorough statistical analysis of existing case studies and algorithmic 
approaches. This comprehensive synthesis provides valuable references for future research, 
enhancing the understanding of the MAED landscape.
(1)	 The growing prominence of MOAs in MAED solutions post-2015 reflects an evolution 
in optimization strategies. This trend is driven by two main factors: the increasing inter­
connectedness of global power systems, which heightens the need for effective MAED 
solutions, and the demonstrated superiority of MOAs over traditional mathematical 
methods in addressing complex engineering challenges, including MAED.
(2)	 Research efforts have predominantly focused on a subset of MAED cases, underscor­
ing the need for broader eXploration. Specifically, Case VIII and Case VI account for 
nearly half of all applications, primarily due to their earlier introduction and manage­
able scale, which offer a favorable balance between problem complexity and solution 
efficiency.
(3)	 Swarm intelligence-based MOAs have emerged as a dominant approach in solving 
MAED problems. This dominance is attributed to the extensive variety of swarm intel­
ligence techniques and the proliferation of new methodologies in recent years, which 
have attracted significant attention for their applicability across diverse optimization 
scenarios.
In the future, some research directions are worthy of further exploration.
(I) MAED model aspect.
(1)Addressing large-scale MAED cases is imperative as power systems continue to 
expand globally. With the growing concept of global power grids and intercontinental 
interconnectors (Brinkerink et al. 2019), future research should prioritize the develop­
ment of effective solutions for large-scale cases, such as Case IV, Case V, Case X, and 
Case XI.
(2)The importance of multi-area environmental economic dispatch (MAEED) will 
intensify in the context of global carbon neutrality. As industries increasingly focus on 
low-carbon goals, environmental economic dispatch models in power systems, which 
aim to balance economic efficiency with environmental sustainability, will become 
ever more critical.

(5)Accounting for reserve constraints is vital in maintaining system reliability across

(II) Solution methods aspect.
(1)	 A comparative analysis of MOA performance across MAED cases is essential for 
informed decision-making. Given the variability in effectiveness among different 
MOAs, a detailed comparative study that evaluates their performance across all eleven 
reported MAED cases is crucial. Such an analysis is necessary to offer practical rec­
ommendations for selecting appropriate solution methods, providing a foundation for 
optimizing MAED problem-solving strategies. This comprehensive comparison will be 
extensively covered in Part II of this series.
(2)	 Enhancing computational efficiency is critical as MAED models scale up. As the sys­
tem scale expands, the computational efficiency of solving large-scale MAED cases 
may diminish. To address this, future research should focus on the development and 
application of high-performance computing methods, such as distributed computing, 
parallel computing, and GPU acceleration, which are necessary to meet the practical 
requirements of timely dispatching solutions within the 15-min operational window.
(3)	 Developing more sophisticated multi-objective MOAs is vital for handling complex 
MAED problems. As models increasingly on multi-area environmental economic dis­
patch with renewable energy and energy storage system, they will evolve into larger-
scale, multi-objective problems with intricate constraints, necessitating the creation of 
more effective and efficient multi-objective algorithms.

Abstract: Multi-area economic dispatch (MAED) provides an indispensable component for the secu­ rity and economic operation of contemporary power systems. Over recent years, numerous metaheuristic optimization algorithms (MOAs) have surfaced for addressing the MAED problem. However, none of the literature to date conducted a comprehensive statistical research work on the MAED problem. In part I of this series, we present a comprehen­ sive survey on this problem. (1) We collect all eleven reported MAED cases studied over the years. These cases have different structures, scales, and constraints. We illustrate the structures of all cases and provide their corresponding system parameters. (2) We collect all the MOA solution algorithms. These algorithms are inspired by different ways, and we categorize them in detail and review them comprehensively. (3) We list the detailed ap­ plications of MOAs on different cases and count the percentage of studies on each case. (4) Finally, we summarize the current research progress and point out the future research directions in terms of MAED models and solution methods, respectively. This survey pro­ vides an extensive overview of the MAED cases and its solution methods. It can provide applicable and reference suggestions for future research on the MAED problem.
